title: Fix and flex the seven aspects in a scenario
blurb: Apply PRINCE2 Agile's fix and flex defaults to a scenario's trade-offs, and name which performance aspect a statement describes.
question: Pinewick cannot fit lockers into all 20 largest stores before Easter within budget. What should flex, and what must stay fixed?

teach.body: Formally: PRINCE2 sets performance targets and tolerances for seven aspects: benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk. PRINCE2 Agile's defaults (Table 3.1) fix time and cost with zero tolerance and flex what is delivered. In plain English: the date and the budget do not move; you protect the essentials and the minimums, and you adjust the nice-to-haves.

head: Aspect
Fixed
Flexed
teach.caption: These five rows are the ones exam questions turn on. Quality and risk tolerances are also set, but this lesson does not key on their rows.

teach.h: Which aspect is the statement about? (1.3.2)
head: Aspect
Meaning
Stem cue
rows: Characteristics making products fit for purpose
What will and will not be delivered

root.label: Forecast: the plan will not fit

teach.h: Benefits and sustainability: fixed floor, flexible ceiling

teach.body: Managing by exception in agile means allowing tolerance on what is delivered and restricting it on time and cost. If the team forecasts that even the Must haves, or the minimum benefits, cannot be delivered within the fixed time and cost, that is beyond tolerance: an exception for the project board, not a quiet change by the project manager.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 5.1, Table 3.1

items: Strike out any option that moves the date or adds money.
Strike out any option that falls below the minimum benefits or minimum sustainability criteria.
Prefer the option that drops or defers Should or Could work.
If Must haves cannot fit, the answer is an exception, not a hidden cut.

teach.body: Pinewick Home and Garden's board fixes the £1.6 million budget and the Easter date. Click and collect live in all 85 stores is a Must have; the board allows lockers at fewer than the 20 largest stores, so locker numbers flex. If the board sets reusable crates as Pinewick's minimum sustainability criterion, cheaper cardboard is out. The finance director's call for evidence of extra sales, not just channel shift, is about benefits.

teach.text: Classic traps: time and cost never flex by default, so 'delay to protect scope' is wrong. A cheaper supplier that misses the minimum sustainability standard is not acceptable, and splitting the work with that supplier still breaks it. 'A baseline improvement with room for more' is the benefits target, not quality or scope. Seven aspects, not the old six-sided hexagon.

items: Time and cost: zero tolerance at every level of plan.
Scope: Musts fixed; Should and Could flexed.
Benefits fixed at minimum viability; sustainability fixed at minimum criteria; both flex above.
Musts or minimums forecast to miss: exception to the board.

summary: You can now apply PRINCE2 Agile's fix and flex defaults to a scenario: protect time, cost, Must haves and the minimum benefits and sustainability criteria, and flex everything above them. You can also say which performance aspect a statement describes.

A.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's board has fixed the £1.6 million budget and the Easter go-live, and has agreed that lockers may go into fewer than the 20 largest stores. The project manager now forecasts that lockers in all 20 stores cannot be finished in time within budget. What should the project manager do?
options: Ask the board for extra budget so all 20 locker stores are completed
Move the Easter go-live to May so that every planned locker fits
Reduce the number of locker stores and keep the date and budget
Pause the store roll-out until the locker supplier can catch up
A.why: Time and cost have zero tolerance; scope is flexed for Should and Could haves, and the board has made locker numbers flexible (Table 3.1).

whyNot.0: Cost has zero tolerance on all levels of plan.
whyNot.1: Time has zero tolerance; Easter cannot move.
whyNot.3: Pausing the roll-out delays the fixed date.

A.q: At Pinewick's project canvas workshop, the finance director says click and collect must at least show a measurable rise in total sales, not just sales moving between channels, and that any rise above that would be welcome. Which aspect is being discussed, and how is it handled by default?
options: Scope, fixed for Must haves and flexed for the others
Benefits, fixed at minimum viability and flexed above it
Sustainability, fixed at minimum criteria and flexed above
Cost, held at zero tolerance on all levels of the plan
A.why: Benefits are measurable improvements the business expects; Table 3.1 fixes them for minimum viability and flexes anything above (1.3.2, Table 3.1).

whyNot.0: Scope is what will and will not be delivered, not the improvement expected.
whyNot.2: Sustainability is about impact on the wider environment.
whyNot.3: Cost is fixed, but the discussion is about the improvement in sales.

A.q: Pinewick's sustainability strategy sets reusable crates as the minimum standard for collection orders. A packaging supplier offers cardboard boxes that would save £60,000, and the e-commerce team's remaining budget is tight. What is the MOST appropriate response?
options: Switch to cardboard boxes so that the project stays within budget
Use cardboard in half of the stores and crates in the other half
Delay the locker roll-out until the cost of the crates comes down
Keep reusable crates and drop lower-priority Should or Could work
A.why: Sustainability is fixed for its minimum criteria; to stay within fixed cost, flex Should and Could scope instead (Table 3.1).

whyNot.0: Cardboard falls below the minimum sustainability criteria, which are fixed.
whyNot.1: Splitting still breaks the minimum criteria in half of the stores.

B.q: Pinewick's head of store operations says that each store's stock accuracy must reach at least 97% before click and collect goes live there, or customers will arrive to find items missing. Which performance aspect does this statement describe?
options: Benefits
Scope
Quality
Risk
B.why: Quality is the set of characteristics that make the project's products fit for purpose and in line with expectations (1.3.2); 97% accuracy is a standard the service must meet.

whyNot.0: Benefits are the measurable improvements the business expects from the change.
whyNot.1: Scope is what will and will not be delivered, not the standard it must meet.
whyNot.3: The statement sets a required standard rather than describing an uncertainty.

B.q: Pinewick's e-commerce team forecasts that, if it builds every planned feature for the Release 2 pilot, the pilot will go live two weeks late. Gift messages and saved favourites are Could haves. Which response fits PRINCE2 Agile's defaults?
options: Drop or defer the Could have features so the pilot is on time
Let the pilot slip by two weeks, within the stage's time margin
Add two contractors so all features fit, using spare budget
Shorten payment security testing to recover the two weeks
B.why: Time has zero tolerance; scope flexes for Should and Could haves (Table 3.1).

whyNot.1: Time has zero tolerance at every level of plan, so there is no margin to use.
whyNot.2: Cost has zero tolerance at every level of plan.
whyNot.3: Cutting security testing threatens a product standard the board has very low appetite to risk.

B.q: Pinewick's board says click and collect must be live in all 85 stores before Easter, but lockers may be installed at fewer than the 20 largest stores if necessary. How should these two requirements be classified?
options: Store coverage is flexed scope; locker numbers are fixed scope
Store coverage is a benefit; locker numbers are a quality criterion
Both are time tolerances, as both depend on the Easter date
Store coverage is fixed scope; locker numbers are flexed scope
B.why: Scope is fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should and Could haves (Table 3.1); the board has made all 85 stores a Must and locker numbers flexible.

whyNot.0: This reverses them: the board made coverage essential and lockers flexible.
whyNot.1: Both describe what will be delivered, which is scope.
whyNot.2: Time is the Easter date itself; these describe what is delivered by then.

C.q: Pinewick's project manager forecasts that online payment, a Must have, cannot be ready in all stores by Easter within budget. He proposes quietly moving it into an after-Easter update without telling the project board. Is this an appropriate application of fix and flex, and why?
options: Yes, because scope is the aspect that flexes in an agile project
Yes, because the project manager manages each release day to day
No, because Must haves are fixed, so this forecast is an exception
No, because payment features are in the stock supplier's contract
C.why: Scope is fixed for Must haves (Table 3.1); a forecast that Musts cannot be delivered within time and cost is beyond tolerance and goes to the board as an exception.

whyNot.0: Scope flexes for Should and Could haves, not Must haves.
whyNot.1: The PM manages within tolerances; a forecast breach must be escalated.
whyNot.3: The stem gives no such contract term; the problem is a fixed Must have missing.

C.q: Pinewick's board sets zero tolerance on time and cost for every level of plan, but allows the number of locker stores and the less important website features to vary. Is this an appropriate application of fix and flex, and why?
options: Yes, because the default fixes time and cost and flexes what is delivered
Yes, because lockers are a Must have for each of the larger stores
No, because tolerances should be set on time and cost, not on scope
No, because zero tolerance leaves the project manager no room to manage
C.why: PRINCE2 Agile allows tolerance on what is delivered and restricts it on time and cost (Table 3.1, Table 5.1).

whyNot.1: The board has made lockers flexible, so they are not a Must have.
whyNot.3: The room to manage comes from flexing scope.

C.q: Pinewick has met its minimum sustainability criteria with reusable crates. The team proposes adding electric vans for moving crates between stores, which would cut emissions further but push Release 3 two weeks past Easter. Is this an appropriate proposal, and why?
options: Yes, because sustainability above the minimum should be maximized
Yes, because the budget still has room to pay for the extra vans
No, because sustainability is not one of the seven performance aspects
No, because work above the sustainability minimum flexes and time is fixed
C.why: Sustainability is fixed for minimum criteria and flexed above them; time has zero tolerance, so extra sustainability work cannot push the date (Table 3.1).

whyNot.0: Above the minimum, sustainability is flexible, not something to maximize at any cost.
whyNot.1: Budget is not the problem; the proposal breaks the fixed time.
whyNot.2: Sustainability is one of the seven aspects in PRINCE2 7 and PRINCE2 Agile V2.

reteach.title: Date and money fixed; extras flex
reteach.question: Can you choose the trade-off that respects the defaults?

blocks.body: Time and cost do not move. Musts, minimum benefits and minimum sustainability criteria are protected. Everything else, Should and Could work and anything above the minimums, is where you flex. If even the protected items cannot fit, raise an exception.

blocks.text: Delaying or adding money is never the default fix. Below-minimum sustainability is not acceptable even if cheaper.

explain.body: PRINCE2 Agile's default is zero tolerance for extra time and extra cost on all levels of plan: project, stage and team.

test.q: Pinewick's store operations team is running two weeks behind on staff training for the pilot stores. Its Kanban lead suggests asking for a two-week extension to the stage. What does PRINCE2 Agile's default say about time?
options: A two-week margin is allowed at stage level
Extra time is allowed at team plan level
There is zero tolerance on all levels of plan
Time may flex when cost stays within budget
test.why: Table 3.1: zero tolerance for extra time on all levels of plan.

whyNot.0: No time margin is allowed by default at any level.
whyNot.1: Team plans also have zero time tolerance.
whyNot.3: Time and cost are both fixed; neither trades against the other.

explain.body: Scope is fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should and Could haves. When work will not fit, drop or defer Coulds first, then Shoulds.

test.q: Pinewick's e-commerce team cannot finish all Release 1 stories. Which stories should it drop first?
options: The Must have stock display for each store
The Could have stock alerts by text message
The Must have accessibility fixes for the stock page
The Must have link to the Tallis stock system
test.why: Scope flexes for Should and Could haves; Coulds go first (Table 3.1).

whyNot.2: Must haves are fixed, and accessibility is essential for this service.

explain.body: Benefits: fixed for minimum viability, flexed above. Sustainability: fixed for minimum criteria, flexed above. A cheaper option that falls below either minimum is not acceptable.

test.q: Pinewick wants click and collect to cut wasted car journeys and packaging, with reusable crates as the minimum standard. Which performance aspect is this?
options: Benefits
Sustainability
Quality
Scope
test.why: Sustainability is how the project will impact the wider environment (1.3.2); fixed for minimum criteria (Table 3.1).

whyNot.0: Benefits are the measurable business improvements, such as extra sales.
whyNot.2: Quality is about products being fit for purpose.
whyNot.3: Scope is what will and will not be delivered.

explain.body: Benefits: measurable improvement. Quality: characteristics that make products fit for purpose. Scope: what will and will not be delivered. Sustainability: impact on the wider environment.

steps.label: Ask: improvement, standard, content or environment?

test.q: Pinewick's board states that home delivery will not be part of this project; only collection from stores and lockers is included. Which aspect does this statement define?
options: Scope
Quality
Sustainability
Benefits
test.why: Scope is what the project will deliver and what it will not deliver (1.3.2).

whyNot.1: Quality is about how fit for purpose the products are.
whyNot.2: Sustainability is about impact on the wider environment.
whyNot.3: Benefits are improvements the business expects, not what is in or out.
